page_title: Build a simple 2D physics engine for JavaScript games

sources.entry: JavaScript: _Build a simple 2D physics engine for JavaScript games_

summary.title: Build a simple 2D physics engine for JavaScript games
summary.one_liner: You learn how to structure a lightweight rigid-body 2D physics engine in JavaScript (entities, position/velocity updates, AABB collision detection, and displacement/elastic collision resolution) as an alternative to heavier libraries like Box2D.
takeaways: A physics engine can be decomposed into entities, a collision detector, a collision solver, and an engine that runs them each game-loop step.
Position and velocity are updated over elapsed time using p(n+1)=v*t+p(n) and v(n+1)=a*t+v(n).
Rectangle (AABB) collision can be tested by checking whether any edge lies beyond the other rectangle's edges.
Elastic resolution repositions the entity at the collision edge and reflects velocity scaled by a restitution coefficient, with a small threshold to stop jitter.
Simpler engines reduce CPU usage per frame, which matters for 30-60 FPS canvas games, but lack features of mature libraries like Box2D.
summary.summary: The article walks through building a small rigid-body 2D physics engine in JavaScript for a platformer, explaining why a home-grown engine can beat a library like Box2D on CPU cost. It covers choosing features, a real-time game loop driven by requestAnimationFrame, and a physics entity holding position, velocity, acceleration, size, and restitution data. It then describes a rectangle collision detector and a solver with displacement and elastic resolution, with code snippets for each part. The page text cuts off partway through the elastic resolution code, so the remainder of the article is not covered.
